items.gold: Get the TMS report, match in FBL1N, post with FB50 to G/L 4711000, and set the reversal for the 1st of the month.
items.answer:

- Ana matches each line in FBL1N and drops already-invoiced shipments [11][1].

items.q: Why were deliveries 80419876 and 80419902 included in the October accrual even without a POD?
items.gold: The carrier (Nordline) confirmed delivery on 29.10 by mail.
items.answer:
Deliveries 80419876 and 80419902 (Nordline, Hamburg) were included under a one-time October exception, not the standard rule.

- **Standard rule:** Accruals select shipments by actual POD date up to the cut-off, and shipments with no POD in the TMS are not part of the normal run [1].
- **Why they were included:** Both had no POD in the TMS. The carrier confirmed delivery by mail on 29.10, and Tom Hendriks included them on that basis [9][6].
- **Approval:** Ana Novak approved including them on 30.10, citing the carrier mail [7].
- **Scope:** The exception applies to the October run only. No general rule has been set for future runs, and POD remains the standard basis [1][3].
- **Not in sources:** The individual amounts for these two deliveries.

Each claim (POD-date standard rule, Tom Hendriks including them, Ana Novak's 30.10 approval, October-only scope) is supported by sources [1], [3], [6], [7], and [9]. items.q: Why did Antwerp choose a dispatcher check before loading instead of a check at the gate?
items.gold: The gate only checks driver ID and delivery number, and a dispatcher check before loading also avoids reloading a truck that cannot leave.
items.answer:
Antwerp chose a dispatcher check because the gate check would not have caught the problem, and the dispatcher stage comes earlier.

- The gate only verifies driver ID and delivery number, so it would not catch a missing printed DGD [2][5].
- A dispatcher check happens before loading, so trucks that cannot leave are not loaded and then reloaded [1][5].
- The trigger was two UN 1263 cases (29 and 30 Sep 2026). Trucks were held about 2.5 hours with no printed DGD. The DGDs existed in SAP but were never printed [2][5].
- Marta Kowalska first thought of a gate check [8], then agreed to the dispatcher check on 8 Oct, effective 12 Oct [6][1]. The sources do not show a gate check as decided [1][3].

Note: the wiki status says the cause is not recorded [3], but Sofie Peeters's 5 Oct email states it

judge.reason: The answer gives both reference facts: the gate only checks driver ID and delivery number, and a dispatcher check before loading avoids reloading trucks that cannot leave. Its other claims (the two UN 1263 cases, the 8 Oct agreement, the 12 Oct effective date, and the gate check not being decided) are supported by the cited sources.

items.q: What caused the DGDs for the two UN 1263 shipments to be missing?
items.gold: They existed in SAP but were not printed because the print job went to the wrong printer in the office.
items.answer:
- Sofie Peeters reported on 5 Oct that the DGDs for both UN 1263 shipments existed in SAP but were never printed, because the print job went to the wrong office printer [5][1].
- The declarations were created, so the fault was in printing, not creation [9].
- The gate check only verifies driver ID and delivery number, so it would not have caught a missing printed DGD [1][9].
- The emails do not separate the two deliveries, so the printer explanation is the reported cause for both.
- Caveat: the wiki status page (21 Oct) says the cause is not yet recorded and that Marta Kowalska's question to Sofie had no reply by then [11]. Treat the printer explanation as reported but not yet confirmed.

judge.reason: The answer states the reference's key fact: the DGDs existed in SAP but were not printed because the print job went to the wrong office printer. Each claim is supported by the cited sources, including the caveat that the wiki status page says the cause is not yet recorded.

items.q: When does the new ADR dispatcher check rule start and where is it recorded?
items.gold: From Monday 12 Oct, in a checklist in the WMS.
items.answer:
- **Start date:** Monday 12 Oct 2026. Marta Kowalska set the rule effective that day on 8 Oct 2026 [6]. The WMS checklist went live that morning [8].
- **Start condition:** No dangerous goods (ADR) are loaded without a dispatcher check of the printed, signed DGD, recorded in a five-item WMS checklist [6].
- **Where it is recorded:** The wiki page "ADR transport document check before loading (task; outbound-delivery)". Its "How to do it" section gives the agreement date and the 12 Oct start [1]. Its "What it is" section gives the rule [2]. Its "Status" section confirms the checklist has been live since 12 Oct [3].
- The wiki and emails agree on the date. The 8 Oct date is the agreement date, not the start date.

judge.reason: The answer gives the start date as Monday 12 Oct 2026 and states the rule is recorded in a WMS checklist, matching the reference. Each claim is supported by the cited emails [6], [8] and wiki sections [1]-[3].

items.q: Which deliveries were found without ADR documents?
items.answer:
Two Antwerp deliveries were found at the dock without ADR transport documents (dangerous goods declarations):

- **80451233**: 12 pallets, UN 1263 (paint, class 3), found 29 Sep 2026 [1][3][12]
- **80451290**: 8 pallets, UN 1263 (paint, class 3), found 30 Sep 2026 [1][3][12]

In both cases the trucks were held about 2.5 hours until the paperwork was printed. Nothing left without documents [3][12].

Cause: Sofie Peeters reports the DGDs existed in SAP but were never printed, because the print job went to the wrong office printer [1][8]. The wiki status page says the cause is not yet recorded [3], so the sources disagree.
